searchDocs.title: linear​
searchDocs.content: </> Splynx.linear( points: {VectorLike}?,-- Relative to the pivot. pivot: VectorLike?-- Defaults to the origin. ) → LinearSpline Straight segments between the points. Needs at least two points to make a segment.

searchDocs.title: bezier​
searchDocs.content: </> Splynx.bezier( points: {VectorLike}?,-- Relative to the pivot. pivot: VectorLike?-- Defaults to the origin. ) → CubicSpline Cubic Bezier curves: points 1-4 make the first curve, 4-7 the second, and so on, so it passes through every third point. Points past the last complete curve are kept but ignored.

searchDocs.title: hermite​
searchDocs.content: </> Splynx.hermite( points: {VectorLike}?,-- Relative to the pivot. velocities: {VectorLike}?,-- One per point. Missing ones are zero. pivot: VectorLike?-- Defaults to the origin. ) → CubicSpline Passes through every point, leaving each one with its velocity. Change velocities withCubicSpline:setVelocity.

searchDocs.title: cardinal​
searchDocs.content: </> Splynx.cardinal( points: {VectorLike}?,-- Relative to the pivot. scale: number,-- How strongly the curve follows its neighbours; 0.5 is Catmull-Rom. pivot: VectorLike?-- Defaults to the origin. ) → CubicSpline Passes through every point, with velocities of (next - previous) * scale. The end points mirror their only neighbour. Change the scale with CubicSpline:setScale.

searchDocs.title: catmullRom​
searchDocs.content: </> Splynx.catmullRom( points: {VectorLike}?,-- Relative to the pivot. pivot: VectorLike?-- Defaults to the origin. ) → CubicSpline A Splynx.cardinal spline with a scale of 0.5: passes through every point with natural-looking curves.

searchDocs.title: bSpline​
searchDocs.content: </> Splynx.bSpline( points: {VectorLike}?,-- Relative to the pivot. pivot: VectorLike?-- Defaults to the origin. ) → CubicSpline A uniform cubic B-spline: smooth everywhere, including across joints, but it only passes near its points. Needs at least four points.

searchDocs.title: rounded​
searchDocs.content: </> Splynx.rounded( points: {VectorLike}?,-- Relative to the pivot. reach: number | {number},-- How far either side of every corner the rounding starts and ends, or one per point. Missing ones are 0. pivot: VectorLike?-- Defaults to the origin. ) → CubicSpline Straight lines between the points, with the corner at each point rounded off by a circular arc. The arc startsreach studs before the corner and ends reach studs after it, whatever the angle, so sharper turns get tighter arcs. Unlike Splynx.catmullRom, the straight parts stay straight, so it suits paths laid out from waypoints. The ends and corners with a reach of 0 stay sharp. For arcs of a set radius instead, use Splynx.filleted. Where the arcs at both ends of a line would need more of it than there is, both shrink in proportion until they meet, so a reach is the most a corner gets. A path that doubles back on itself turns sharply. Arcs are cubic approximations, within about 0.03% of their radius for a right angle. Its curves alternate between lines and arcs, starting and ending with a line. Change reaches withCubicSpline:setRadius. local path = Splynx.rounded({ Vector3.new(0, 0, 0), Vector3.new(40, 0, 0), Vector3.new(40, 0, 30), }, 2)

searchDocs.title: filleted​
searchDocs.content: </> Splynx.filleted( points: {VectorLike}?,-- Relative to the pivot. radius: number | {number},-- The arc radius of every corner, or one per point. Missing ones are 0. pivot: VectorLike?-- Defaults to the origin. ) → CubicSpline Like Splynx.rounded, but each corner is an arc of radius. An arc of the same radius needs more room the sharper the turn: it starts radius * tan(turn / 2) studs before the corner, the radius at a right angle and about 3.7 times it at a 150 degree turn. Where there isn't that much room, the arc shrinks to fit, which also shrinks its radius.

searchDocs.title: sampled​
searchDocs.content: </> Splynx.sampled( source: LinearSpline | CubicSpline,-- The spline to copy. spacing: number,-- Studs between samples, along the spline. keepJoints: boolean?-- Put a sample on every joint, so sharp corners stay sharp. ) → SampledSpline A static copy of source as straight segments spacing studs apart along it, for the fastest distance lookups. Smaller spacing follows curves more closely. It doesn't follow later edits to source; sample it again after changing it. Samples that land either side of a sharp corner cut across it. With keepJoints, every joint (see getJoints) gets a sample, and each curve is split into equal segments no longer than spacing, so a linear spline's corners and a rounded spline's straight lines come out exact. Lookups cost the same either way.

searchDocs.title: Errors
searchDocs.content: Type	Description"Spacing must be more than 0"	If `spacing` isn't positive. "Spline doesn't have enough points to make a curve"	If `source` has no curves.

searchDocs.title: Segments​
searchDocs.content: </> interface Segments { points: {vector}-- The samples, relative to the pivot. There's one more than there are segments. directions: {vector}-- Each segment's direction, as a unit vector. Segments with no length borrow a neighbour's. distances: {number}-- How far along the spline each sample is. count: number-- The number of segments. } A sampled spline's own data, frozen so it can be shared instead of copied. See SampledSpline:getSegments.

searchDocs.title: getOffsetPosAtDistance​
searchDocs.content: </> SampledSpline:getOffsetPosAtDistance( distance: number,-- Studs from the start. Clamped to the length. offset: number,-- Studs to the right of the direction of travel; negative is to the left. hint: number?-- Ignored: there's no search to speed up. Accepted so calls match the other splines. ) → ( vector,-- The offset position. vector,-- The spline's direction of travel there, as in SampledSpline:getDirectionAtDistance. number-- The segment index, in place of a hint. ) The position offset studs to the side of the spline, distance studs along it, for things that walk beside the path instead of on it. The side is horizontal, so the height stays the spline's. Straight up or down has no horizontal side, so there it keeps the side of the nearest part of the spline that isn't vertical: a climb that bends up and over in one vertical plane keeps the same side the whole way. Offset positions jump a little at each sample where the direction changes, by about offset * angle. Smaller spacing makes the jumps smaller.

searchDocs.title: getSegments​
searchDocs.content: </> SampledSpline:getSegments() → Segments The samples, segment directions and distances the spline is made of, for building your own lookups on top of it. They're the spline's own lists, frozen rather than copied, so this costs nothing. Points are relative to the pivot. local segments = sampled:getSegments() local pivot = sampled:getPivot() for i = 1, segments.count do local from = pivot + segments.points[i] local direction = segments.directions[i] local length = segments.distances[i + 1] - segments.distances[i] end

searchDocs.content: </> CubicSpline:getJoints() → {vector} Where each curve starts, plus where the last one ends. For Bezier splines these are every third point; for B-splines they're between the points.

searchDocs.title: getCurveCount​

searchDocs.title: getJointDistances​
searchDocs.content: </> CubicSpline:getJointDistances() → {number} How far along the spline each of CubicSpline:getJoints is: 0, then the end of each curve.

searchDocs.content: </> CubicSpline:getPoints() → {vector}-- Relative to the pivot. A copy of the points. Change them through CubicSpline:setPoint and friends so the spline stays up to date.

searchDocs.title: setPoints​
searchDocs.content: </> CubicSpline:setPoints( points: {VectorLike}-- Relative to the pivot. ) → () Replaces every point. Hermite splines keep their velocities in order, adding zero velocities for new points, and rounded splines do the same with their radii.

searchDocs.title: addPoints​
searchDocs.content: </> CubicSpline:addPoints( points: {VectorLike},-- Relative to the pivot. velocities: {VectorLike}?-- Hermite splines only: one per added point. Missing ones are zero. ) → () Adds points to the end. Existing curves keep their tables unless the new points change them. On a rounded spline the new points get the radius it was made with, or 0 if it was made with a list of radii.
